title: Particles fired one at a time still build up wave stripes
body: Send electrons, photons or even molecules at two narrow slits one at a time, and each one lands on the screen as a single dot. Yet as thousands arrive, the dots pile up into bright and dark stripes: an interference pattern, the signature of overlapping waves. Quantum mechanics describes each particle with a wave that passes through both slits and sets the odds of where it lands. Detect which slit each particle takes, and the stripes disappear.

slides.alt: Animation of a dark detector screen behind two slits. Particles arrive one at a time as green phosphor dots that look random at first, then build up into many bright stripes. Wave crests spread from both slits and an intensity curve matches the stripes; with which-slit detectors the stripes vanish.

slides.prompt: Fire particles one at a time until stripes appear. Then change the colour or the gap, or watch which slit each one takes.
slides.takeaway: Each particle lands as a single dot, yet together they draw interference stripes. Watch the slits and the stripes vanish: only the blurred single-slit glow is left.

slides.heading: One spot each
slides.text: Every particle is detected at a single point, never smeared out. Quantum mechanics predicts only the odds: the squared size of the wave at each place on the screen. Physicists still disagree about how to picture what happens between source and screen.

events.text: G. I. Taylor uses very dim light

slides.heading: Look, and it vanishes
slides.text: Detect which slit each particle goes through, and the pattern becomes the sum of two single-slit patterns, with no interference stripes. A 1987 experiment found that partial which-path information could be gathered without wiping the interference out completely.

slides.question: The largest molecules shown to interfere so far: roughly how many atoms in each?
slides.explanation: About 2,000 atoms, with a mass of about 25,000 daltons, in 2019. Buckyballs of 60 carbon atoms interfered in 1999, molecules of 810 atoms in 2013.

slides.question: What happens to the stripes if you detect which slit each particle goes through?
slides.explanation: With which-path information the interference is gone: the pattern becomes the sum of two single-slit patterns, without stripes.
